ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.
This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of Basque Center on Cognition, Brain, and Language.

Lastly, the study did not directly manipulate experimenter presence: participants were unsupervised at home, while an experimenter was present in the lab to ensure protocol compliance, introducing a potential confound between environment and supervision.
One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study.
Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men).
All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.
Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

In the supervised group, participants were accompanied by the same experimenter in both environment: when in the lab, they were welcomed and seated in an experimental booth equipped with a camera and microphone for technical assistance; at home, they remained observed by the experimenter via Zoom, with their camera and microphone active throughout the session.
In the home environment, participants were permitted to use any available microphone, including both laptop-integrated and externally mounted devices.
Participants were asked to respond aloud as soon as the stimulus appeared and while it was displayed on the screen.
Finally, participants completed Cheek and Melchior's (1990) shyness questionnaire.
All participants completed both a laboratory and a home session and may thus have become familiar with the protocol.
Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study. Five were excluded because they did not complete both sessions, and one was excluded because of recording issues. The final sample size was 96. Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men). Based on the effect sizes reported in previous research for vowel space expansion (ηₚ² = 0.12-0.65; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004), we estimated that to reach 90% power for between-subject comparison, we needed 24 participants. For other variables, following Brysbaert & Stevens, (2018), an effect of ~15 ms would require about 1,600 observations per condition to reach 80% power. With 96 participants, our design yielded more than 5,100 observations for VOT and CoG in each condition (e.g., HF-home-supervised). These observation counts, which exceed the recommended threshold, provide high statistical power even accounting for potential data loss or effects smaller than 15ms (see detailed power analysis description in pre-registration (https://osf.io/yx3e7), and Data availability and Supplementary Material for details and the complete power analysis). In order to account for personality differences that could influence competence under supervision, we administered a 13-item questionnaire on personality type (Melchior & Cheek, 1990) to determine, for each participant, whether they tended to be more or less shy and show inhibition in the presence of others. Shyness was chosen as a straightforward measure of social comfort that plausibly can influence supervised speech performance, and it correlates with related constructs such as social anxiety and extraversion (Cheek & Buss, 1981). We used the ζ-Overlapping test, in R (Pastore, 2018; Pastore & Calcagnì, 2019; Perugini et al., 2024) with permutation-based inference to compare density distribution of the two groups and estimate exact p-values. This method is assumption-free and computes the exact probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed (Perugini et al., 2024). Comparing shyness scores did not yield a significant difference between supervision groups (p = .072). All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee. Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Online and onsite experiment comparison of acoustic features in speech production research.
table.research_questions:
Despite recent dramatic improvements in web technology, some criticism and prejudices toward online behavioral experiments persist. Many researchers have questioned such intrinsic limits of online approach and examined differences in the outcomes between online and onsite (lab-based) experiments (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020; de Leeuw & Motz, 2016; Hilbig, 2016). Nevertheless, some recent research showed consistency and comparability between online and onsite RT measures, which suggests that online experiments can be reliably used in psycholinguistic research. On the other hand, other fields of psycholinguistics and cognitive sciences that employ other measures than RTs (e.g., speech onset times, acoustic analyses of speech) cannot yet fully rely on web-based experiments, partly, because of the lack of comparisons with traditional methods. In addition, speech production is not studied uniquely with naming latency: there is a vast part of cognitive sciences that study speech production employing acoustic analysis instead. Crucially, investigation on the adequacy of online recording of speech production for acoustic analysis purposes has apparently never been investigated in a controlled fashion. We intend to explore whether studies on speech production can be moved online by comparing online and onsite environments.
Since the literature reports that the lexical frequency effect in reading is smaller (12-15ms) than the effect in naming (45-50ms; see Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), we aim to employ both tasks to measure with finer grain size two levels of online experiments sensitivity (without directly comparing them). We expect to replicate the robust results of lexical frequency (shorter SOT for HF words vs. LF words) in both online and onsite experiments; also, both environments will elicit comparable effects in both the reading and the naming tasks. If this will be the case, we can assume that online experiments are a suitable tool for detecting both large and small latency differences and that the online solutions can be used without substantial limitations.

We will also explore the effect of lexical frequency over acoustic features in both online and onsite environments. Regarding these features, we expect to find more hyperarticulated vowels and longer consonant VOT in the LF words compared to the HF words, with no difference between online and onsite conditions. Such results on vowel hyperarticulation and VOT would be in line with previous onsite studies (Munson, 2007; Munson and Solomon, 2004; VanDam & Port, 2005), which however never employed a picture naming task to investigate the influence of lexical frequency on acoustic features. The results that explored SOT with both tasks suggest, however, that the naming task will elicit the same pattern as reading aloud. Fricative COG modification has never been investigated in relation to lexical frequency effect, thus it is an open question whether fricatives will show higher COG with LF words than HF words.

We expect to observe differences between the Supervised and the Unsupervised groups independently of the experimental environment (and possibly depending on participants personality). Because of a more relaxed circumstance, we expect that the Unsupervised group will have longer SOTs, which would be in line with Fairs & Strijker’s (2021) explanation for their results on longer latencies in online testing (see also Belletier & Camos, 2018; Palmer et al., 2019; Guerin, 1986). Accordingly, we expect a reduced difference between LF and HF words regarding vowel space and VOT duration as compared to the Supervised group. If our expectation is confirmed, we would conclude that participants’ behavior mostly depends on the supervision and future online studies should carefully take this in consideration.
In line with the idea that both unsupervised and online sessions entail less controlled environments, we might observe an interaction between Supervision*Environment factors, which would lead to longer SOT, less hyperarticulated vowels, shorter plosive VOT (and possibly lower fricative COG) in the unsupervised-online session, as compared to the other conditions (Unsup-Online > Unsup-Onsite > Superv-Online = Superv-Onsite). However, the present literature does not allow us to draw strong predictions.

table.sample_size:
Our target sample size is two groups of 48 Spanish speakers. We will attempt to recruit 100 participants assuming that there might be some technical problems or some of the participants may not complete all the sessions. All participants will be paid for their time. 
We will recruit a total of 100 native speakers of Spanish, aged 18-35, with low or medium-low proficiency in any other language, to form two groups of 50 each. The two groups of participants will be matched for age, L2 proficiency and education level.
table.measured_variables:
For each trial (in both tasks) we will measure Speech Onset Time. 
Based on the three vowels (/i/,/a/,/u/) we are using for our stimuli, we will measure the vocalic space (over the three corner vowels).
Depending on the initial consonant of each word-trial, we will measure either the Voice Onset Time (for plosives) or the Center of Gravity (for fricatives). 
All the plosive consontants will be analyzed together as a single group.
All the fricative consontants will analyzed as another independent group.
table.statistical_tests:
We will examine the SOT of trials in relation to the variables Lexical Frequency, Supervision, and Environment. We will inspect our data and remove outliers before testing our hypotheses. We will use linear mixed effect models and use SOT as the dependent variable; Word Frequency (High F. vs Low F.), Supervision (Supervised vs Unsupervised) and Environment (Online vs Onsite) as fixed effects. Initially a minimal structure of random effects (allowed by the experimental design) will be used. Where possible, we will introduce by-subject and by-item random effects (i.e., subject random intercept). Also, we will modify and adjust the model to guarantee the best fit to our data. To identify the best model for our analysis, we will specify various random effects structure and compare models fit with the "Performance" package in R. If any interaction between fixed effects will be detected, that will be further explored by using emmeans package (Tukey HSD test).

The same procedure will be followed for consonant VOT, COG, and vowel space (vowel hyperarticulation). Regarding the latter, we will not conduct a by-item analysis, because this dependent variable can only be calculated by participant. 

To investigate whether the two groups of participants (Supervised and Unsupervised) differ in terms of shyness, which could be a confounding factor, we will run an independent samples Bayesian t-test using the individual results of the shyness test as dependent variable.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will discard missed or wrong answers - e.g., use of incorrect target name during the picture naming task. 
During data pre-processing, we will discard from acoustic analysis those trials that are too noisy or disturbed.

For SOT, VOT and COG, we will only discard values that are 2.5 standard deviation above or below individual mean. Regarding the vowel space analysis, we will also inspect individual distribution and consequently remove outliers. This is important for vowel analysis to ensure that the values fall within the acceptable values for each vowel category.
table.missing_data_handling: If a subject does not complete one of the two sessions (Online/Onsite), that subject will not be included in the analysis. Conversely, if they complete only one of the two tasks (but in both sessions), that subject will be included in the analysis of that task.
table.exploratory_analyses: As part of exploratory analyses, we will introduce the shyness questionnaire individual scores as random intercept of our main models and explore whether shyness influences online and onsite experiment performance.

table.sample_size_rationale:
Vowel space: 
Power analysis was conducted based on the effect size calculated on vowel space in LF and HF words of previous onsite studies (Munson, 2007; Munson and Solomon, 2004). The effect size in Munson (2007) was ηp2 = 0.45, whereas in Munson & Solomon (2004) was ηp2 = 0.57 (F1). In order to detect the lexical frequency effect on vowel space with 90% of power, we would need 16 participants for within subject conditions (ANOVA within factors,  alpha = .05, non-sphericity correction = 1)  and 24 (in total) for between conditions (ANOVA between factors, alpha = .05, correlation among repeated measurements = 0.5). 
We ran this exploratory F1 power analysis to know the minimum number of participants we need for detecting a difference in vowel space between HF and LF words across conditions. But, given the fact that we are going to use a different statistical test and given that online testing might introduce more variability, we intend to collect data from two groups of 50 participants (in line with Fairs & Strijker, 2021). 

Other dependent variables: 
The reported power analysis aimed to provide F1 result, indicating the number of participants to measure the vowel space only. Conversely, to decide the number of trials of the other dependent variables, we relied on Brysbaert & Stevens (2018), who suggest that for an effect of 15ms, 1,600 observations per condition are enough to reach 80% of power. Importantly, this number can be distributed across participants and/or trials (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018; see also Keuleers et al., 2012). For instance, Keuleers et al., (2012) reached 80% of power for such an effect of lexical frequency with 40 participants and 40 trials per condition. 
The SOT difference between HF and LF is expected to be about 15ms in the reading task (45-50ms in the naming task) (see Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), thus we can rely on the threshold Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. The studies that explored the effect of lexical frequency on plosive VOT found that LF words have a VOT that is roughly 10 ms longer than HF words (VanDam & Port, 2005). Given that this effect size is 5 ms smaller than that of SOT, the number of observations should be (proportionally) raised to ~2100 within each level (across participants and trials). Since there are no studies on lexical effects in fricatives, we will simply use the same number of trials as for the plosive group. 
By recruiting two groups of 50 participants each (100 participants total), we will be able to collect 5,400 observations for the SOT variable, 2,700 observations for the plosive VOT variable, 2,700 for the fricative COG variable in each factor and condition (i.e., 2,700 in the HF-online-supervised condition). This numbers, which are widely above the recommended 1,600 observations, guarantee high statistical power even in the case of some invalid participants and data loss. 

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]
table.stopping_rule:
We aim to recruit 100 participants to account for possible data loss and have a final sample size of about 92/96 valid participants (~46/48 each group). If we reach 96 valid participants before testing all the 100 participants, we will stop collecting data. If, once all the 100 participants are tested, the number of valid participants is below 46 per group (92 total), we will recruit more participants until reaching at least 46 valid participants per group, allowing us to collect enough data points, as Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. In fact, 46 participants will allow the collection of ~2480 observations for both consonant groups and of ~4900 observations for the SOT variable.

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]
table.manipulated_variables:
We will use bi/three-syllabic HF and LF Spanish words; in each of the two tasks there will be 54 HF and 54 LF words, which will be repeated twice for a total of 216 trials per task [UPDATED 36 HF and 36 LF words repeated three times. 216 total]. The reading task and the naming task will not use the same words to avoid too many repetitions, which would reduce the lexical frequency effect across sessions.
We will use words with the onset being either a plosive (/p/, /t/, /d/) or a fricative consonant (/s/, /f/). There will be 6 words per plosive in the HF condition and 6 in the LF condition (12 words per /p/, /t/, /d/, 36 in total). Due to Spanish orthophonological rules, we can only use two fricatives (/f/ and /s/), so we selected 9 words per fricative in the HF condition and 9 in the LF condition (18 words per /f/ and /s/, 36 in total). Each word will be repeated three times (36 words x 2 consonant groups x 3 repetitions = 216 trials). We will use the corner vowels /i/, /a/, /u/, that will be used to measure participants’ vowel space. From the total number of trials, each vowel will be contained in 72 word-trials of each session and per participant (36 word trials x 2 HF/LF x 3 vowels).

Please read:
[The final design used 36 unique HF and 36 LF words per task, each repeated three times (216 trials total). This adjustment from the initial plan maintained the same total number of trials, thus preserving the intended statistical power.]
table.study_design_overview:
We will run two separated tasks: picture naming and reading aloud. 
Each one will have a 2x2x2 design: one between-subject factor, Supervision, with two conditions (Supervised and Unsupervised), and two within-subject factors, Word Frequency (High Frequency/Low Frequency) and Environment (Online/Onsite environment). Both Supervised and Unsupervised group of participants will be tested on both the Online and the Onsite conditions on two separated days (total number of sessions: 2). The order of the Environment and of the tasks (Reading and Naming) will be counterbalanced across participants.

[Updated names for publication: Home and Lab (instead of Online and Onsite)].
table.data_collection_procedures:
Each participant will be tested in two sessions, one onsite (in the lab) and one online (at home). Depending on the group (Supervised or Unsupervised), the participants will be either supervised by the experimenter in both the online and onsite sessions or not. 

The order of the sessions will be counterbalanced across participants. Each session will be carried out on different days and  there will be a 6-12 days break between two consecutive sessions. We will use PCIbex (Zehr, Schwarz, 2018), a browser-based tool, to administer the experiment in both the online and the onsite sessions.

In the online sessions, participants will receive a link to the experiment and will be informed that they will be needing a working microphone (either integrated or external) to carry out the tasks. In the onsite sessions, participants will be provided with a headset with microphone.

Participants will be asked to complete the experiment in one go, although they are allowed to have breaks. In both groups and sessions, one screening question will directly query if the participants are alone in a quiet room and if so they will be for the whole duration of the experiment. After that, they will carry out a self-quality check of the recording; if they consider that the output has sufficient quality they will be allowed to proceed. 

The Supervised condition will entail the presence of an experimenter who will interact with the participants and inform them the experimenter will be listening and help in case of any problem. For the Supervised group, during the online condition, the interaction will happen via an online conference platform. The same experimenter will be present at both online and onsite (supervised) sessions. 

For both Supervised and Unsupervised groups, the same instruction and screening tests will appear on the screen at the beginning of the sessions. Also, the same experimental instruction will be used for both Onsite and Online conditions. 

The order of the two tasks will be counterbalanced across participants, half of them will begin with the picture naming task and half with the reading task. In the reading task, the participants will see “+” at the centre of the screen for 500ms at the beginning of each trial, followed by a written word for 2000ms. They will have to read aloud each word before the time runs out and the word disappears. They will not receive any instruction on how to pronounce those words; they will only know that they are being recorded. Each word will appear in three separated blocks and presented in a randomized order. 
In the picture naming task, the participants will be first familiarized with the images to ensure naming agreement. Then the main task will follow the same procedure as in the reading task. 

In order to account for personal shyness, comfort with supervision and interaction with experimenters, we are going to administer a short questionnaire at the end of the 2nd session, based on Cheek's (1983) shyness test (see also Cheek & Buss, 1981). By doing so, we will investigate participants’ shyness and determine how they feel regarding supervised and online experiments.

In order to detect the lexical frequency effect on vowel space with 90% of power, we would need 16 participants for within subject conditions (ANOVA within factors, alpha = .05, non-sphericity correction = 1) and 24 (in total) for between conditions (ANOVA between factors, alpha = .05, correlation among repeated measurements = 0.5).
We ran this exploratory F1 power analysis to know the minimum number of participants we need for detecting a difference in vowel space between HF and LF words across conditions. But, given the fact that we are going to use a different statistical test and given that online testing might introduce more variability, we intend to collect data from two groups of 50 participants (in line with Fairs & Strijker, 2021).

Other dependent variables:
The reported power analysis aimed to provide F1 result, indicating the number of participants to measure the vowel space only. Conversely, to decide the number of trials of the other dependent variables, we relied on Brysbaert & Stevens (2018), who suggest that for an effect of 15ms, 1,600 observations per condition are enough to reach 80% of power. Importantly, this number can be distributed across participants and/or trials (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018; see also Keuleers et al., 2012). For instance, Keuleers et al., (2012) reached 80% of power for such an effect of lexical frequency with 40 participants and 40 trials per condition.
The SOT difference between HF and LF is expected to be about 15ms in the reading task (45-50ms in the naming task) (see Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), thus we can rely on the threshold Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. The studies that explored the effect of lexical frequency on plosive VOT found that LF words have a VOT that is roughly 10 ms longer than HF words (VanDam & Port, 2005). Given that this effect size is 5 ms smaller than that of SOT, the number of observations should be (proportionally) raised to ~2100 within each level (across participants and trials). Since there are no studies on lexical effects in fricatives, we will simply use the same number of trials as for the plosive group.
By recruiting two groups of 50 participants each (100 participants total), we will be able to collect 5,400 observations for the SOT variable, 2,700 observations for the plosive VOT variable, 2,700 for the fricative COG variable in each factor and condition (i.e., 2,700 in the HF-online-supervised condition). This numbers, which are widely above the recommended 1,600 observations, guarantee high statistical power even in the case of some invalid participants and data loss.

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]", "We aim to recruit 100 participants to account for possible data loss and have a final sample size of about 92/96 valid participants (~46/48 each group). If we reach 96 valid participants before testing all the 100 participants, we will stop collecting data. If, once all the 100 participants are tested, the number of valid participants is below 46 per group (92 total), we will recruit more participants until reaching at least 46 valid participants per group, allowing us to collect enough data points, as Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. In fact, 46 participants will allow the collection of ~2480 observations for both consonant groups and of ~4900 observations for the SOT variable.

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]", "We will use bi/three-syllabic HF and LF Spanish words; in each of the two tasks there will be 54 HF and 54 LF words, which will be repeated twice for a total of 216 trials per task [UPDATED 36 HF and 36 LF words repeated three times. 216 total]. The reading task and the naming task will not use the same words to avoid too many repetitions, which would reduce the lexical frequency effect across sessions.
We will use words with the onset being either a plosive (/p/, /t/, /d/) or a fricative consonant (/s/, /f/). There will be 6 words per plosive in the HF condition and 6 in the LF condition (12 words per /p/, /t/, /d/, 36 in total). Due to Spanish orthophonological rules, we can only use two fricatives (/f/ and /s/), so we selected 9 words per fricative in the HF condition and 9 in the LF condition (18 words per /f/ and /s/, 36 in total). Each word will be repeated three times (36 words x 2 consonant groups x 3 repetitions = 216 trials). We will use the corner vowels /i/, /a/, /u/, that will be used to measure participants’ vowel space. From the total number of trials, each vowel will be contained in 72 word-trials of each session and per participant (36 word trials x 2 HF/LF x 3 vowels).

This adjustment from the initial plan maintained the same total number of trials, thus preserving the intended statistical power.]", "We will run two separated tasks: picture naming and reading aloud.

Both Supervised and Unsupervised group of participants will be tested on both the Online and the Onsite conditions on two separated days (total number of sessions: 2). Depending on the group (Supervised or Unsupervised), the participants will be either supervised by the experimenter in both the online and onsite sessions or not.

The order of the sessions will be counterbalanced across participants. Each session will be carried out on different days and there will be a 6-12 days break between two consecutive sessions. We will use PCIbex (Zehr, Schwarz, 2018), a browser-based tool, to administer the experiment in both the online and the onsite sessions.

In the online sessions, participants will receive a link to the experiment and will be informed that they will be needing a working microphone (either integrated or external) to carry out the tasks. In the onsite sessions, participants will be provided with a headset with microphone.

Participants will be asked to complete the experiment in one go, although they are allowed to have breaks. The Supervised condition will entail the presence of an experimenter who will interact with the participants and inform them the experimenter will be listening and help in case of any problem. For the Supervised group, during the online condition, the interaction will happen via an online conference platform. The same experimenter will be present at both online and onsite (supervised) sessions.

For both Supervised and Unsupervised groups, the same instruction and screening tests will appear on the screen at the beginning of the sessions. Also, the same experimental instruction will be used for both Onsite and Online conditions.

The order of the two tasks will be counterbalanced across participants, half of them will begin with the picture naming task and half with the reading task. In the reading task, the participants will see “+” at the centre of the screen for 500ms at the beginning of each trial, followed by a written word for 2000ms. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p-values > .05", Text = "No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

ownership.dep_title: Online and onsite experiment comparison of acoustic features in speech production research.
ownership.dep_description: This study aims to test whether online (web) and onsite (lab) experiments are comparable and can interchangeably be used for speech production research. With the present experiment we wish to provide a landmark on online experiment reliability for future web-based research on speech production that uses the measures of speech production that include speech onset time (SOT), vowel formant frequencies, voice onset time (VOT) in prevocalic plosives, and center of gravity (COG) of prevocalic fricatives. Therefore, we are going to repeat the same tasks in both environments and compare the magnitude of the frequency effect on both naming latencies and acoustic measurements. We are going to add the presence/absence of an experimenter supervision as a further factor. Thanks to this, we will ascertain whether the difference between lab and online experiments, if any, must be attributed to supervision, rather than the experimental environment. We will use two tasks, reading aloud and picture ...

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.
This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of Basque Center on Cognition, Brain, and Language.
live_data_statements: Lastly, the study did not directly manipulate experimenter presence: participants were unsupervised at home, while an experimenter was present in the lab to ensure protocol compliance, introducing a potential confound between environment and supervision.
One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study.
Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men).
All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.
Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

In the supervised group, participants were accompanied by the same experimenter in both environment: when in the lab, they were welcomed and seated in an experimental booth equipped with a camera and microphone for technical assistance; at home, they remained observed by the experimenter via Zoom, with their camera and microphone active throughout the session.
In the home environment, participants were permitted to use any available microphone, including both laptop-integrated and externally mounted devices.
Participants were asked to respond aloud as soon as the stimulus appeared and while it was displayed on the screen.
Finally, participants completed Cheek and Melchior's (1990) shyness questionnaire.
All participants completed both a laboratory and a home session and may thus have become familiar with the protocol.
Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

text.text: Remote online experiments are increasingly popular in psycholinguistics, yet their suitability for speech acoustics remains debated.
This preregistered study tested whether speech collected online at home reproduces laboratory patterns, and whether an experimenter's presence matters.
Ninetysix native Spanish speakers completed picture-naming and reading-aloud tasks once in the lab and once at home (both browser-based), with or without an experimenter.
We measured vowel space, plosive voice onset time (VOT) and fricative center of gravity (CoG), and tested lexical frequency effects on each measure across environments and supervision groups.

Compared with the lab, voiceless VOT was shorter at home and CoG was markedly higher, the latter likely reflecting recording artifacts; vowel space was smaller at home in reading, with a similar but non-significant difference in naming.
Home-lab agreement of individual speakers' values was good for voiced VOT, moderate for vowel space and voiceless VOT, and poor for CoG.
Lexical frequency did not affect VOT or CoG.
High-frequency words elicited larger vowel spaces than low-frequency words in naming in both environments, but only at home in reading.
Stimulus examination revealed that phonological neighborhood density was confounded with lexical frequency.
Exploratory analyses showed that high-density words elicited larger vowel spaces in all conditions and tasks, although the effect was somewhat smaller at home.
Critically, experimenter supervision had no effect on any measure in either task.

Thus, unsupervised home recording can capture group-level effects on vowel space, whereas absolute VOT values should not be compared across environments, and CoG is not recommended without controlled recording equipment.

Although online experimentation dates back to the late '90s (e.g., Givaty et al., 1998; Hecht et al., 1999), its widespread adoption in psycholinguistic research emerged only in recent years, driven by advances in the internet speed, browser quality, and the accessibility of web-based experimental platforms (see Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although online experimentation dates back to the late '90s (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Givaty et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hecht et al., 1999)</ref>, its widespread adoption in psycholinguistic research emerged only in recent years, driven by advances in the internet speed, browser quality, and the accessibility of web-based experimental platforms (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These developments have made online testing increasingly appealing for behavioral research, offering efficient data collection, larger and more diverse samples, and greater statistical power while reducing logistical and financial costs (Henrich et al., 2010; Kimball et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2021).

text.text: Some criticism regarding the time resolution and consistency of online measurementsattributed to differences in internet speed, device quality, operating systems, and browsers (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020) has been raised in chronometric research.

text.text: However, a substantial body of work shows that, despite the above concerns, classical effects, such as lexical frequency and semantic interference, replicate online, with effect sizes comparable to those obtained in the laboratory environment, for both manual responses and vocal response latencies (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020; Bürki, 2025; Fairs & Strijkers, 2021; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026; Vogt et al., 2021).

text.text: Therefore, online data collection seems to be a suitable setting for psycholinguistic research focusing on manual response and speech latencies.

Crucially, however, speech production is not studied exclusively by measuring naming latencies; acoustic measures -including vowel formants (indexing vowel quality and vowel space expansion), voice onset time (VOT) of plosives, and center of gravity (CoG) of fricatives are central tools for characterising speech production and understanding the cognitive processes that shape it (Burnham et al., 2010; Kalashnikova & Carreiras, 2021; Peng et al., 2010; Piazza et al., 2023; 2025; Rodriguez-Cuadrado et al., 2018; Stoehr et al., 2017; Wikse Barrow et al., 2022; Zheng & Samuel, 2020).

text.text: Formants represent the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract (Lagefoged, 2006), with the first two formans (F1 and F2) characterizing most of the oral vowels.
text.formatted: Formants represent the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract <ref type="bibr">(Lagefoged, 2006)</ref>, with the first two formans (F1 and F2) characterizing most of the oral vowels.

text.text: VOT refers to the time between the release of a plosive consonant and the onset of vocal cord vibration (Liberman et al., 1967 , Lisker & Abramson, 1964), and typically voiced and voiceless plosives display distinct VOT values.
text.formatted: VOT refers to the time between the release of a plosive consonant and the onset of vocal cord vibration <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Liberman et al., 1967</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">, Lisker & Abramson, 1964)</ref>, and typically voiced and voiceless plosives display distinct VOT values.

text.text: CoG represents the frequency-weighted average of a fricative's spectral energy, reflecting articulatory differences in the production of some fricatives, as, for example, /s/ and /f/ (Jongman et al., 2000).
text.formatted: CoG represents the frequency-weighted average of a fricative's spectral energy, reflecting articulatory differences in the production of some fricatives, as, for example, /s/ and /f/ <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jongman et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike response latencies and speech onset time (SOT), it is still unclear whether these measures collected remotely, in home or online environments, are comparable to those obtained under controlled laboratory conditions.
In this preregistered study, we tested whether psycholinguistic experiments based on acoustic measures of speech yield similar results when conducted in participants' homes and in the lab.
Crucially, both sessions were run on the same online platform (PCIbex), with recordings saved in the same format (WebM).
text.formatted: Crucially, both sessions were run on the same online platform (PCIbex), with recordings saved in the same format <ref type="bibr">(WebM)</ref>.

text.text: This allowed us to examine within-subject effects of the testing environment while holding the recording software and file format constant.

Given that most commercially available microphones now record speech at high quality, and that sound-card differences mainly affect timing rather than recording quality, we did not expect technical factors to change the acoustic measures substantially.

Any home-lab differences should therefore mainly reflect the recording environment (e.g., background noise, room reverberation), the microphones used at home, or speaker-related factors, such as a more relaxed speaking style or less psychological stress at home (Stoehr et al., 2023).

text.text: Spanish phonetics provides a clear framework for examining our research questions.

The Spanish vowel system comprises five monophthongs (/a, e, i, o, u/) with relatively stable formant structure and limited coarticulatory variability compared to English (Bradlow, 1995), making vowel formants a suitable measure of Spanish vowel quality for comparison purposes.
text.formatted: The Spanish vowel system comprises five monophthongs (/a, e, i, o, u/) with relatively stable formant structure and limited coarticulatory variability compared to English <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bradlow, 1995)</ref>, making vowel formants a suitable measure of Spanish vowel quality for comparison purposes.

text.text: Voiceless stops in Spanish (/p, t, k/) are produced with no aspiration (Lisker & Abramson, 1964; Cho & Ladefoged, 1999), whereas voiced stops (/b, d, g/) are produced with prevoicing (Lisker & Abramson, 1964; Rosner et al., 2000; Souganidis et al., 2024), reflected in clearly distinct distributions of positive and negative VOTs, respectively.
text.formatted: Voiceless stops in Spanish (/p, t, k/) are produced with no aspiration <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lisker & Abramson, 1964;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cho & Ladefoged, 1999)</ref>, whereas voiced stops (/b, d, g/) are produced with prevoicing <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lisker & Abramson, 1964;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rosner et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Souganidis et al., 2024)</ref>, reflected in clearly distinct distributions of positive and negative VOTs, respectively.

text.text: Fricatives such as /s/ and /f/ vary on the measure of CoG: /s/ typically exhibits a high CoG and concentrated spectral energy, while /f/ shows a diffuse, low-frequency spectrum (Jongman et al., 2000).

text.text: These measures have been previously investigated as windows into underlying cognitive processes linked to articulatory planning.

By leveraging these acoustic features, the present study can assess the viability of online psycholinguistic studies focusing on speech production in varying tasks (reading and naming) and supervision groups (with supervision or without, see below).
Relocating testing outside the laboratory reduces control over the recording environment.
Variations in microphone type, background noise, room acoustics, and speaker distance across homes can alter the absolute values of acoustic measurements.

Accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, a large body of research has evaluated the quality of remote acoustic data collection, including the use of online conferencing platforms such as Zoom (Calder et al., 2025). Zhang et al. (2024), for example, compared laboratory-grade equipment (a portable recorder with a professional headset) with remote methods (a smartphone application and Zoom), all recorded in participants' homes.

(2024)</ref>, for example, compared laboratory-grade equipment (a portable recorder with a professional headset) with remote methods (a smartphone application and Zoom), all recorded in participants' homes.

text.text: They found that fundamental frequency was comparable across all conditions, with smartphone recordings most closely approximating the high-quality reference recordings (see also Oganyan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They found that fundamental frequency was comparable across all conditions, with smartphone recordings most closely approximating the high-quality reference recordings (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oganyan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, lab and home recordings have not been directly compared in detail, and it is uncertain whether high recording quality guarantees comparable acoustic measurements across environments.
Moreover, other acoustic features remain untested.
Psycholinguistic research is increasingly moving online, with speech researchers being similarly enthusiastic about remote methods.

Nevertheless, benchmarking research is needed to systematically delineate both the possibilities and the limitations of online approach to psycholinguistic research on the acoustic measures of speech.

To the best of our knowledge, only one published study has investigated differences in speech measures between online and in-lab environments (Stoehr et al., 2023). Stoehr et al. (2023) conducted a picture naming task in Spanish, Basque, and English, comparing participants' VOT, vowel formants, and vowel duration in a lab (with and without surgical masks) and online home environment.
text.formatted: To the best of our knowledge, only one published study has investigated differences in speech measures between online and in-lab environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Stoehr et al., 2023)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Stoehr et al. (2023)</ref> conducted a picture naming task in Spanish, Basque, and English, comparing participants' VOT, vowel formants, and vowel duration in a lab (with and without surgical masks) and online home environment.

text.text: They found that, in both home and lab conditions, L3 English VOT was significantly longer than Spanish and Basque VOT for voiceless plosives, showing that both environments (even with surgical masks) can detect cross-language VOT differences (~12-15 ms).
Note that these differences in VOT are already substantial in the lab, indicating that large effect sizes can be replicated online using temporal acoustic features like VOT.
However, it is unclear whether smaller effect sizes or within-language manipulations can be replicated with online methods.
The authors also observed that VOT was overall shorter in online recordings compared to lab-based.
This effect of the environment raises important questions about whether measurements obtained online are directly comparable to those gathered in traditional laboratory environments.

In the same study, Stoehr and colleagues (2023) analyzed the vowel space -determined by the peripheric vowels /a-i-u/ -of Spanish and Basque (combined) to examine whether it differs between home and lab testing environments.
text.formatted: In the same study, <ref type="bibr">Stoehr and colleagues (2023)</ref> analyzed the vowel space -determined by the peripheric vowels /a-i-u/ -of Spanish and Basque (combined) to examine whether it differs between home and lab testing environments.

text.text: Although they found a wider Spanish-Basque vowel space at home than in the lab--suggesting that environment affected absolute acoustic values--it remains unclear whether within-experiment effects on spectral features can be observed in home environment with similar success as in the lab.

Lastly, the study did not directly manipulate experimenter presence: participants were unsupervised at home, while an experimenter was present in the lab to ensure protocol compliance, introducing a potential confound between environment and supervision.
Another fundamental difference between laboratory and home testing is the experimenter presence.

Research on social presence suggests that an observer can both enhance performance, through social facilitation, whereby the presence of others promotes participants' performance (Rosenthal, 1976; Uziel, 2007; Zajonc, 1965), and impair it on tasks requiring executive control, where monitoring induces self-awareness and performance pressure (Belletier et al., 2015; Belletier & Camos, 2018; Palmer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Research on social presence suggests that an observer can both enhance performance, through social facilitation, whereby the presence of others promotes participants' performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rosenthal, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Uziel, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Zajonc, 1965)</ref>, and impair it on tasks requiring executive control, where monitoring induces self-awareness and performance pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belletier et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Belletier & Camos, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Palmer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, the role of experimenter supervision in the expression of psycholinguistic effects has not been directly manipulated for acoustic-phonetic measures, as most of previous studies focused on chronometric outcomes (either reaction time or SOT).

For instance, Hilbig (2016), in a lexical decision task, replicated the classical lexical frequency effect (i.e., high frequency words elicit faster responses than low frequency words) in a fully controlled lab setting, web-based experiment in the lab, and a fully web-based experiment conducted online with no experimenter' monitoring.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hilbig (2016)</ref>, in a lexical decision task, replicated the classical lexical frequency effect (i.e., high frequency words elicit faster responses than low frequency words) in a fully controlled lab setting, web-based experiment in the lab, and a fully web-based experiment conducted online with no experimenter' monitoring.

text.text: This may suggest that the absence of an experimenter has no impact on the results (similar findings by Ollesch et al., 2006).

text.text: However, supervision was not manipulated independently of the environment (lab/home), thus confounding the effects of environment and presence of supervision. Piazza et al. (2026) addressed this limitation by crossing environment (home vs. lab conditions) and supervision (supervised vs. unsupervised conditions) in speech-production tasks.

(2026)</ref> addressed this limitation by crossing environment (home vs. lab conditions) and supervision (supervised vs. unsupervised conditions) in speech-production tasks.

text.text: In picture naming, the lexical frequency effect was robust and comparable in both supervised and unsupervised groups (~29-40 ms).
In reading aloud, the frequency effect emerged in both groups and environments, except in the home-supervised condition.

Importantly, overall, both home-/labunsupervised conditions yielded the largest effect sizes, suggesting that experimenter presence may subtly dampen frequency effects, possibly via increased self-monitoring, and that these effects are more salient in home environments, where supervision might be experienced as unusual.
Supervision can therefore modulate small psycholinguistic effects, manifested in smaller differences in SOT (i.e., planning times) between high frequency (HF) and low frequency (LF) words.
It remains uncertain whether dampening effects of supervision extend to spectro-temporal features of speech sounds, such as formants, VOT, or CoG.

By crossing supervision with environment, the present design examines whether differences in speech acoustics between home and lab environments are due to the physical setting or the presence of an experimenter.
The lexical frequency effectone of the most robust effects in psycholinguisticsis characterized by faster recognition or naming of HF words as compared to LF ones.
It has been found in various experimental designs, in both written and pictured word recognition (e.g., reading aloud or picture naming; Zipf, 1929; see Brysbaert et al., 2011 for a review).
text.formatted: It has been found in various experimental designs, in both written and pictured word recognition (e.g., reading aloud or picture naming; <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Zipf, 1929;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Brysbaert et al., 2011</ref> for a review).

text.text: The effect is generally attributed to more efficient lexical access: frequently encountered words have higher resting activation levels, making them easier to retrieve (Navarrete et al., 2006).
text.formatted: The effect is generally attributed to more efficient lexical access: frequently encountered words have higher resting activation levels, making them easier to retrieve <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Navarrete et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Its ubiquity and reliability have established the frequency effect as a standard benchmark for validating new methods, and recent studies have demonstrated its successful replication online for response latencies (Bürki, 2025; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Its ubiquity and reliability have established the frequency effect as a standard benchmark for validating new methods, and recent studies have demonstrated its successful replication online for response latencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bürki, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hilbig, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Piazza et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond response latencies, lexical frequency has been reported to influence the acoustic quality of speech (Aylett & Turk, 2006; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004; Tomaschek et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Beyond response latencies, lexical frequency has been reported to influence the acoustic quality of speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aylett & Turk, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Munson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Munson & Solomon, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tomaschek et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Kawamoto et al. (1999) and Gahl (2008) observed shorter duration of the initial phoneme in HF words as compared to LF words. Munson (2007) and Munson & Solomon (2004) found that vowels in HF words were produced more centrally than in LF words, resulting in smaller vowel spaces in HF words. VanDam and colleagues (2009) and VanDam and Port (2005) reported shorter VOT of voiceless plosives in HF than LF words in word reading (~11ms; see Stuart-Smith et al., 2015; Yao, 2009 for similar results in spontaneous speech).

(1999)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Gahl (2008)</ref> observed shorter duration of the initial phoneme in HF words as compared to LF words. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Munson (2007)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Munson & Solomon (2004)</ref> found that vowels in HF words were produced more centrally than in LF words, resulting in smaller vowel spaces in HF words. <ref type="bibr">VanDam and colleagues (2009)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">VanDam and Port (2005)</ref> reported shorter VOT of voiceless plosives in HF than LF words in word reading (~11ms; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stuart-Smith et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Yao, 2009</ref> for similar results in spontaneous speech).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that word frequency impacts production beyond speech planning, affecting the acoustic quality of speech sounds, where high frequency words produced less "pricesely": with shorter onsets, shorter VOTs and reduced vowel spaces.

While our primary aim is to examine differences (if any) in acoustic speech production measures between lab and home environments and based on supervisor presence, we use the lexical frequency effect as a benchmark to test whether it is detected with comparable effect size across environments and supervision conditions.

In this study, we compared vowel space, plosives' VOT, and fricatives' CoG in speech production tasks collected in the lab versus at home (within-participants) environment and with or without experimenter supervision (between-participants), in two tasks: picture naming and reading aloud.

This preregistered design and hypotheses (available here https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YX3E7) forms part of a wider project on online psycholinguistic methods, whose first installment examined SOT (Piazza et al., 2026); the present study examines the spectral and temporal properties of speech sounds.
text.formatted: This preregistered design and hypotheses (available here <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YX3E7">https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YX3E7</ref>) forms part of a wider project on online psycholinguistic methods, whose first installment examined SOT <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Piazza et al., 2026)</ref>; the present study examines the spectral and temporal properties of speech sounds.

text.text: Our primary aim is to assess differences in the acoustic measures of speech, in reading and naming, when collected at home, as compared to the lab (both online), and whether the presence of supervision affects them.

More specifically, we asked, first, whether the acoustic measures of speech overall differ between home and lab environments, possibly arising from microphone, computer, and background-noise differences; and second, whether supervision modulates any of those measures or interacts with the environment.

Since the home sessions and the unsupervised group both entail less experimental control, this least controlled condition (unsupervised-home) might diverge most (as with SOT, see Piazza et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Since the home sessions and the unsupervised group both entail less experimental control, this least controlled condition (unsupervised-home) might diverge most (as with SOT, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Piazza et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, and thirdly, regardless of differences between the environments, we examined whether within-subject psycholinguistic effects remain similarly detectable in both environments and supervision groups.

We used lexical frequency effect and assessed whether the magnitude and the direction on its effect on the acoustic measures of speech differed between environments and supervision groups (Hameau et al., 2021; Mousikou & Rastle, 2015; Sadat et al., 2014; Scarborough, 2013; Wright et al., 2004).
text.formatted: We used lexical frequency effect and assessed whether the magnitude and the direction on its effect on the acoustic measures of speech differed between environments and supervision groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hameau et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mousikou & Rastle, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sadat et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scarborough, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Wright et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Based on previous studies (Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004; VanDam et al., 2009; VanDam & Port, 2005), we expected significant lexical frequency effects, with LF words being produced with larger vowel spaces and longer VOT (with stronger effects in voiceless, cf VanDam et al., 2009) than HF words.
text.formatted: Based on previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Munson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Munson & Solomon, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">VanDam et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">VanDam & Port, 2005)</ref>, we expected significant lexical frequency effects, with LF words being produced with larger vowel spaces and longer VOT (with stronger effects in voiceless, cf <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">VanDam et al., 2009)</ref> than HF words.

text.text: Critically, we expected those effects to be significant in both environments (lab and home), with no Environment × Frequency interaction.

The environment might affect the absolute values, with vowel spaces being smaller and VOTs being longer in the lab than at home (Stoehr et al., 2023), possibly because the formal laboratory environment induces more pronunciation effort and psychological stress than the more relaxed home environment.
text.formatted: The environment might affect the absolute values, with vowel spaces being smaller and VOTs being longer in the lab than at home <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Stoehr et al., 2023)</ref>, possibly because the formal laboratory environment induces more pronunciation effort and psychological stress than the more relaxed home environment.

text.text: Yet, we expected that the magnitude of the lexical frequency effect would remain similar in both environments.

We additionally measured fricatives' CoG to explore their values between environments and supervision groups, and, for the first time, to our knowledge, we explored whether they were modulated by lexical frequency.

Because higher-frequency words are typically produced with reduced articulatory effort (Lindblom, 1990; Aylett & Turk, 2004), we predicted that high lexical frequency would shift fricative CoG toward more central values.
text.formatted: Because higher-frequency words are typically produced with reduced articulatory effort <ref type="bibr">(Lindblom, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Aylett & Turk, 2004)</ref>, we predicted that high lexical frequency would shift fricative CoG toward more central values.

text.text: Two tasks -reading aloud and picture naming (hence naming and reading) -that typically elicit sizable lexical frequency effects were selected for the current study.

Naming yields larger frequency effect sizes than reading aloud (Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), letting us test the sensitivity of our environments to detect strong and weaker effects within the same participants.
text.formatted: Naming yields larger frequency effect sizes than reading aloud <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mousikou & Rastle, 2015)</ref>, letting us test the sensitivity of our environments to detect strong and weaker effects within the same participants.

text.text: It is possible, in fact, that home recordings are suitable for relatively big effect sizes but not for small ones.
Finally, the supervision manipulation is aimed at separating two factors confounded in most of previous research: presence of supervision in the lab and its absence at home.

If supervision induces performance pressure, the unsupervised group would show amplified acoustic measures (larger vowel space, longer VOT, higher CoG) and possibly larger differences between HF and LF words (Piazza et al., 2026).
text.formatted: If supervision induces performance pressure, the unsupervised group would show amplified acoustic measures (larger vowel space, longer VOT, higher CoG) and possibly larger differences between HF and LF words <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Piazza et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Results will clarify whether home-lab differences should be attributed to the environment or to the supervision, and will provide a practical benchmark for collecting speech production data online.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Method</head>

text.text: One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study.
Five were excluded because they did not complete both sessions, and one was excluded because of recording issues.
The final sample size was 96.
Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men).

Based on the effect sizes reported in previous research for vowel space expansion (ηₚ² = 0.12-0.65; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004), we estimated that to reach 90% power for between-subject comparison, we needed 24 participants.

text.text: For other variables, following Brysbaert & Stevens, (2018), an effect of ~15 ms would require about 1,600 observations per condition to reach 80% power.

text.text: With 96 participants, our design yielded more than 5,100 observations for VOT and CoG in each condition (e.g., HF-home-supervised).

These observation counts, which exceed the recommended threshold, provide high statistical power even accounting for potential data loss or effects smaller than 15ms (see detailed power analysis description in pre-registration (https://osf.io/yx3e7), and Data availability and Supplementary Material for details and the complete power analysis).

text.text: In order to account for personality differences that could influence competence under supervision, we administered a 13-item questionnaire on personality type (Melchior & Cheek, 1990) to determine, for each participant, whether they tended to be more or less shy and show inhibition in the presence of others.

text.text: Shyness was chosen as a straightforward measure of social comfort that plausibly can influence supervised speech performance, and it correlates with related constructs such as social anxiety and extraversion (Cheek & Buss, 1981).
