text.text: Comparing shyness scores did not yield a significant difference between supervision groups (p = .072).
All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.
Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.
We used Spanish di/tri-syllabic HF and LF words.
In each task (naming and reading), participants encountered 36 unique HF and 36 unique LF words, repeated three times.

This final count of unique stimuli differs from the preregistration (which specified 54 words repeated twice) due to challenges in identifying a sufficient number of words meeting all selection criteria (specified below).
The total number of trials was kept identical though, maintaining planned statistical power.
Words had CVCV, CVCVCV, or CVCCVCV structure.
Word onsets were either a plosive (/d/, /p/, /t/) 1 or a fricative consonant (/s/, /f/).
There were 12 words per plosive per frequency condition (12 words x 3 plosives x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials).
There were 18 words per fricative per frequency condition (18 words x 2 fricatives x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials).

The vowels in the second position of the words were /a/, /i/, /u/ (for example, tarta, 'cake', piso, 'apartment'; for a complete list of words, see the OSF repository) and were used to draw the vowel triangle and measure participants' vowel space over the three corner vowels of Spanish.
Word stress was always on the first syllable, and the presence of a graphic accent (for the reading task, e.g., página, 'page') was counterbalanced across LF and HF conditions.
There were 24 words per target vowel per frequency level, repeated 3 times (3 vowels x 12 words x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials per environment).
Word frequencies for the Spanish HF and LF words were obtained from the EsPal database (Duchon et al., 2013), which provides comprehensive lexical statistics for Spanish words.
text.formatted: Word frequencies for the Spanish HF and LF words were obtained from the EsPal database <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duchon et al., 2013)</ref>, which provides comprehensive lexical statistics for Spanish words.

text.text: The naming and the reading tasks did not include the same words to avoid potential reduction in the frequency effect due to repetition.
The words used in naming were all concrete whereas some abstract words were used in reading.
The number of concrete and abstract words in reading was matched between the conditions (HF and LF).

Pictures were chosen from the Multipic database (Duñabeitia et al., 2018) and, when not available there, from freely accessible pictures on the internet, (see the Data and Code Availability section for the link to the pictures).
text.formatted: Pictures were chosen from the Multipic database <ref type="bibr">(Duñabeitia et al., 2018)</ref> and, when not available there, from freely accessible pictures on the internet, (see the Data and Code Availability section for the link to the pictures).

text.text: They were colored 300x300 pixel pictures presented on a white background.

1 We included both voiced and voiceless plosives to improve generalizability of the findings and because previously observed effects on voiceless plosive VOT in English (e.g., VanDam et al., 2009), which are aspirated, may differ from those in Spanish, where voiceless plosives are unaspirated.
text.formatted: 1 We included both voiced and voiceless plosives to improve generalizability of the findings and because previously observed effects on voiceless plosive VOT in English (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">VanDam et al., 2009)</ref>, which are aspirated, may differ from those in Spanish, where voiceless plosives are unaspirated.

text.text: For words in each task, we compared the number of letters and syllables between HF and LF words.
We also collected subjective ratings on word imageability and visual complexity (in naming), on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (completely) from 10 native Spanish speakers (5 female).
In all cases, the ζ-Overlapping results showed no significant differences between HF and LF words (see Data availability and Supplementary Material).
Participants in both supervised or unsupervised groups completed two counterbalanced sessions, one conducted in the laboratory and one at home (both online), scheduled 6-12 days apart.
In each session, participants performed both naming and reading tasks, in counterbalanced order.

In the supervised group, participants were accompanied by the same experimenter in both environment: when in the lab, they were welcomed and seated in an experimental booth equipped with a camera and microphone for technical assistance; at home, they remained observed by the experimenter via Zoom, with their camera and microphone active throughout the session.
In both contexts, once the task began, participants could no longer see the experimenter, and all instructions were presented on full screen to ensure similar conditions.
The experimenter did not provide any task-specific guidance, to ensure similar instructions in the supervised and unsupervised groups.
Participants in the unsupervised group completed the tasks without supervisor guidance.

At home, they accessed the study via a link, provided in an email, and performed both tasks within the allotted day (whenever it was more convenient for them); in the lab, they entered a booth where the task was displayed on a laptop's screen, without an experimenter or camera present.
When collecting data in the lab (for both supervised and unsupervised groups), we recorded participants using a Sennheiser HMD 280 Pro headset with a dynamic microphone (-47 dB, 50-13,500 Hz).
In the home environment, participants were permitted to use any available microphone, including both laptop-integrated and externally mounted devices.
Prior to the start of the experiment, they were asked to record a short sentence, play it back, and confirm that the audio quality was satisfactory before proceeding.
Participants reported which microphone and browser they used.
Reading and naming tasks were implemented in PennController for Ibex (Zehr & Schwarz, 2018), a JavaScript-based platform for browser experiments.
text.formatted: Reading and naming tasks were implemented in PennController for Ibex <ref type="bibr">(Zehr & Schwarz, 2018)</ref>, a JavaScript-based platform for browser experiments.

text.text: Recordings were saved in WebM format and converted to WAV offline.
In each task, each trial began with a fixation cue ("+++") for 500 ms, followed by the target word or image for 2000 ms.
Participants were asked to respond aloud as soon as the stimulus appeared and while it was displayed on the screen.
To ensure full capture of the response, recording continued for an additional 500 ms after stimulus offset.
Each stimulus was presented three times, in a pseudorandomized order such that words sharing the same plosive onset did not appear on two consecutive trials, to minimize phonological clustering.
Each task lasted about 20 minutes.
Finally, participants completed Cheek and Melchior's (1990) shyness questionnaire.
Further methodological details about the online recording procedure are reported in Piazza et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Further methodological details about the online recording procedure are reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Piazza et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: All the recordings were phonetically forced aligned to their transcription using easyalign (Goldman, 2011) and phoneme boundaries were manually corrected when necessary.
text.formatted: All the recordings were phonetically forced aligned to their transcription using easyalign <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Goldman, 2011)</ref> and phoneme boundaries were manually corrected when necessary.

text.text: Thus, all target sounds were marked in TextGrid files and extracted by custom scripts in PRAAT software (Boersma & Weenink, 2001).
text.formatted: Thus, all target sounds were marked in TextGrid files and extracted by custom scripts in PRAAT software <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boersma & Weenink, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Then, we computed our dependent variables: vowel space expansion, VOT for plosives, and CoG for fricatives.

Vowel onset was defined as the first glottal pulse showing a clear higher-formant (notably F2) structure in the spectrogram, and offset as the point at which intensity clearly dropped and the formants became less defined at the transition to the following segment.
We examined the first (F1) and second (F2) formant values of the /a/, /i/, /u/ vowel midpoints to calculate vowel space with the package PhonR in R (R Core Team, 2012.
Vowel space area (VSA) was computed as the area of the triangle formed by these three vowels in the F1×F2 plane, using the Shoelace formula: VSA = 0.5

A larger vowel space indicates more peripheral corner vowels Prior to the vowel space calculation, participants' F1 and F2 values were transformed following the Bark method to reduce between-speaker differences in formant estimations due to anatomical differences in the vocal tract (Traunmüller, 1990).
text.formatted: A larger vowel space indicates more peripheral corner vowels Prior to the vowel space calculation, participants' F1 and F2 values were transformed following the Bark method to reduce between-speaker differences in formant estimations due to anatomical differences in the vocal tract <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Traunmüller, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Fricative onset was defined as the appearance of aperiodic high-frequency frication noise, and offset as its cessation at the onset of the following segment.
CoG of /f/, /s/ consonants was extracted from the entire duration of each fricative using the Praat script zero-crossings-and-spectral-moments (v.1.3; Elvira-Garcia, 2014).
Prior to the spectral analysis, a Hann band-pass filter was applied (1,000-11,000 Hz, smoothing 100 Hz).
CoG was then calculated from the power spectrum (power = 2) using Praat's built-in function and a logarithmic transformation was applied to make the two consonants comparable.
VOT was measured manually for the plosives /p/, /t/, and /d/ (among the most extensively studied plosives in psycholinguistic research).

For voiceless plosives, the onset was defined as the release burst of the plosive and the offset as the onset of voicing in the following vowel, identified by the appearance of the first formant (F1).
For the voiced plosive (/d/), prevoicing was measured as negative VOT, with the offset VOT defined as the voicing onset of vowel following the burst.
Voiced plosives in Spanish can be produced as devoiced (i.e., with positive VOT) incidentally (e.g., Souganidis et al., 2024; Stoehr et al., 2023 Stoehr et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Voiced plosives in Spanish can be produced as devoiced (i.e., with positive VOT) incidentally (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Souganidis et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Stoehr et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Stoehr et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Devoiced plosives were discarded from further analyses.

As VOT values for voiced plosives were negative and those for voiceless plosives positive, absolute values were taken to allow a uniform treatment of VOT as an index of articulatory precision across voicing categories, irrespective of direction, to allow consistent comparison between environments and supervision groups (Baayen et al., 2008; see Lo & Andrews, 2015 for discussion).
text.formatted: As VOT values for voiced plosives were negative and those for voiceless plosives positive, absolute values were taken to allow a uniform treatment of VOT as an index of articulatory precision across voicing categories, irrespective of direction, to allow consistent comparison between environments and supervision groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baayen et al., 2008</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lo & Andrews, 2015</ref> for discussion).

text.text: Note that in Spanish voiceless plosives are strictly positive whereas voiced plosives are typically negative (Lisker & Abramson, 1964), which allows us to use the absolute values to regroup the two groups.
text.formatted: Note that in Spanish voiceless plosives are strictly positive whereas voiced plosives are typically negative <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lisker & Abramson, 1964)</ref>, which allows us to use the absolute values to regroup the two groups.

text.text: Smaller values would indicate less precise articulation.
A logarithmic transformation was then applied to the absolute values to normalize the distribution.
All missed and mispronounced words, plosive-initial voiced words produced without prevoicing, and responses with excessive noise were discarded from the analysis.

For each task separately, we removed all responses exceeding 2.5 standard deviations above or below the participant's individual mean (by session) for each variable (in line with previous research using acoustic measures, e.g., Piazza et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For each task separately, we removed all responses exceeding 2.5 standard deviations above or below the participant's individual mean (by session) for each variable (in line with previous research using acoustic measures, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Piazza et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the naming task, missed responses, mispronunciations, responses with excessive background noise, and trials exceeding ±2.5 SD from the participant's mean represented 14.07% of trials for vowels, 8.80% for VOT, and 9.95% for CoG; they were all discarded from further analyses.
In the reading task, the exclusion rates were 9.89% for vowels, 4.13% for VOT, and 1.60% for CoG.
No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05).
text.formatted: No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05).

text.text: The results of the naming and reading tasks were analyzed separately.

For each acoustic feature, we fit linear mixed-effects models with sum-coded Frequency (within-subject HF/LF, contr.sum -1/1); Environment (within-subject home/lab, contr.sum -1/1), Supervision (betweensubject supervised/unsupervised, contr.sum -1/1) and their interactions as fixed effects (see specific formulas in the Results section).

The models for VOT and CoG, respectively, included voicing (/p, t/ vs. /d/, treatment coded, reference: voiced) and fricative (/f/ vs. /s/, treatment coded, reference: /f/) as additional fixed factors.
The preregistration planned to start from a minimal random-effects structure and compare alternative structures with the performance package.
We departed from this plan because building up from a minimal structure risks omitting random slopes required by the design, which inflates Type I error (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: We departed from this plan because building up from a minimal structure risks omitting random slopes required by the design, which inflates Type I error <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Fully maximal structures, on the other hand, are often overparameterized and fail to converge.
We therefore followed the parsimonious approach of Bates et al. (2015).
text.formatted: We therefore followed the parsimonious approach of <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bates et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: We started from a reduced model including only Frequency (plus voicing or fricative), with by-subject and by-item random slopes.

Random slopes explaining less than 1% of the variance in a principal component analysis of the random-effects structure were then removed (see Data availability and Supplementary Material for details).

After finalizing the random structure, as preregistered, for each dependent variable we fit a linear mixed-effects model with Frequency, Environment, Supervision and their interactions as fixed effects (plus voicing in the VOT models and fricative in the CoG models), with the random structure selected as described above.

We then tested whether adding the number of repetitions (NUM_REP; numeric: 0, 1, 2) improved model fit, and retained it only when it did, based on the fit indices of the performance package (AIC, BIC, marginal/conditional R², RMSE; Lüdecke et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We then tested whether adding the number of repetitions (NUM_REP; numeric: 0, 1, 2) improved model fit, and retained it only when it did, based on the fit indices of the performance package (AIC, BIC, marginal/conditional R², RMSE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lüdecke et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The steps to get to the final models can be viewed on the R Markdown available in the OSF repository.
As preregistered, we report the full model, including all interactions, for every measure.
The significance of main effects and interactions was assessed with type II Wald χ² tests (car package;
Fox & Weisberg, 2019).
text.formatted: Fox & Weisberg, 2019).

text.text: Significant interactions were followed up with pairwise comparisons (emmeans package; Lenth et al., 2020), Holm-corrected instead of the preregistered Tukey HSD, which applies no correction when a single two-level contrast is tested.
text.formatted: Significant interactions were followed up with pairwise comparisons (emmeans package; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lenth et al., 2020)</ref>, Holm-corrected instead of the preregistered Tukey HSD, which applies no correction when a single two-level contrast is tested.

text.text: Our research questions concerned both the effect of the environment and whether the lexical frequency effect held in each environment and supervision group.
We therefore also report the Frequency effect (and, in the exploratory analyses, the PND effect) within each Environment and Supervision condition as the model estimate with its 95% CI and Cohen's d.

These per-condition effects are simple effects estimated from the full model and they describe the size and direction of the effect in each condition, but they are not tests of differences between conditions, which are assessed only by the interaction terms.

For this reason, we report them without p-values and do not contrast individual conditions unless the corresponding interaction is significant; the Holm-corrected tests of the per-condition effects are provided in the supplementary material.

text.text: Vowel space.

Phonological Neighborhood Density (PND) is known to affect the quality of speech production: words with high PND yield wider vowel spaces than with low PND words (Munson & Solomon, 2004; Wright, 2004).
text.formatted: Phonological Neighborhood Density (PND) is known to affect the quality of speech production: words with high PND yield wider vowel spaces than with low PND words <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Munson & Solomon, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Wright, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, after observing the unexpected direction of lexical frequency effect on vowel space expansion (HF words showing larger vowel space than LF words), we explored whether the effect was not partially due to higher PND in HF words and lower PND in LF words.
In our stimuli, PND and frequency were correlated, although weakly (Naming task: Spearman's r = .33; Reading task: Spearman's r = .24).
We split the words into High and Low PND (a factor we called cat_PND) based on the EsPal database (Duchon et al., 2013) and re-computed the vowel space measure separately for High and Low PND words.
text.formatted: We split the words into High and Low PND (a factor we called cat_PND) based on the EsPal database <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duchon et al., 2013)</ref> and re-computed the vowel space measure separately for High and Low PND words.

text.text: We followed the same procedure as we employed for the analysis of Lexical Frequency, including the main models and follow-up analyses, all of them being exploratory.
The final formula and the summary table are reported below (Table 5).
text.formatted: The final formula and the summary table are reported below (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: AREA ~ cat_PND x ENVIRONMENT x SUPERVISION + (1 + ENVIRONMENT | SUBJ).
Model Fit: R²m = .058, R²c = .969

This study evaluated the reliability of online experiments for speech production research focusing on the acoustic measures of speech.
Ninety-six Spanish speakers completed a picture naming and a reading aloud task once in the laboratory and once at home, with or without an experimenter's supervision.
We compared three acoustic features: vowel space expansion, VOT of plosives and CoG of fricatives.
First, and primarily, we asked whether these acoustic measures differ between the home and lab environments and between supervised and unsupervised groups.

Second, we asked whether a within-experiment manipulation, lexical frequency, modulates the acoustic measures to a similar extent across environments and groups (that is, if absolute values shift but psycholinguistic effects can still be detected).

Validating online acoustic measurement is timely: while the reliability of web-based chronometric measures has now been extensively documented (e.g., Bürki, 2025; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026), whether the spectral and temporal properties of speech itself can be equally captured outside the laboratory remains largely open (Stoehr et al., 2023).

text.text: Below, we discuss the two research questions in turn, each followed by an interim conclusion, and then consider the implications and limitations for remote speech production research.

Plosive VOT.
In both tasks, VOT was significantly shorter at home than in the lab.

Follow-up exploratory analyses showed that this difference, however, was restricted to voiceless plosives (naming: lab 26 ms vs. home 23 ms; reading: 25 ms vs. 23 ms), whereas the prevoicing of /d/ did not differ between environments.
Similarly to the results for vowel space, the direction matched our preregistered expectation of shorter VOTs in less controlled sessions.

Although this result should be interpreted cautiously, because the stimuli had an unbalanced number of voiced and voiceless consonants (/p, t/ vs. /d/) and the analysis is exploratory, it replicates and extends Stoehr et al. (2023), who examined voiceless plosives (/p, t, k/) and similarly found longer VOTs in the lab than in home recordings of Spanish and Basque speakers.

Importantly, Stoehr and colleagues compared lab recordings (not browser-based) with web recordings, whereas in our study both environments were browser-based, yet we still observed longer lab VOTs for voiceless plosives.
Thus, the effect is unlikely to be due to the browser or recording platform.
It might instead reflect the microphones used at home.

Additional analyses revealed that the home-lab difference did not differ between participants using a mounted versus a laptop-internal microphone at home, even when voiceless plosives were considered alone (see Data availability and Supplementary Material).

However, both types are typically consumer-grade devices, unlike the Sennheiser headset used in the lab, and they may capture the weak, short-lag VOT of Spanish voiceless plosives less well than the strong periodic energy of prevoicing, which would shorten the measured VOT for voiceless plosives only.
Alternatively, the difference may reflect contextual factors such as the more familiar, relaxed home environment, consistent with the smaller vowel spaces at home.
If this is the case, since experimenter supervision had no effect, any such influence is more likely tied to the place itself than to being observed.

At the speaker level, voiceless VOT was only moderately to poorly preserved across environments (ICC(A,1) = .57/.45 for naming/reading), whereas /d/ prevoicing was well preserved (.78/.81; Section 4.4).
Absolute VOT values should therefore not be compared across home and lab recordings, and analyses of voiceless VOT should remain within one environment until further validation is available.
Fricative CoG.

CoG was strikingly higher at home than in the lab for both /f/ and /s/, in both tasks (Cohen's d = 0.39-0.40), and the shift was much larger for /f/, whose CoG almost doubled at home (e.g., naming: 1,823 Hz in the lab vs.
3,641 Hz at home).
Together with the large variability of home values (Figures 3 and 6; Table 1), this pattern points to a recording-condition artifact rather than a genuine change in participants' articulation.
text.formatted: Together with the large variability of home values (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">3</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">6</ref>; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), this pattern points to a recording-condition artifact rather than a genuine change in participants' articulation.

text.text: Fricative spectral measures such as CoG are among the acoustic measures most affected by the recording device, with built-in computer microphones yielding systematically shifted (higher) CoG values (Sanker et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Fricative spectral measures such as CoG are among the acoustic measures most affected by the recording device, with built-in computer microphones yielding systematically shifted (higher) CoG values <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Sanker et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, broadband high-frequency noise present in home environments, such as laptop fans or ambient sound, would shift the spectral CoG upward regardless of the phoneme, and more so for a weak fricative such as /f/, whose own energy is low relative to the noise.
As for VOT, the home-lab difference in CoG did not differ between participants who used a mounted or a laptop microphone at home.

It was also already present among Chrome users (69/81 participants for /f/ and 62/81 for /s/), with the same direction among users of other browsers (see Data availability and Supplementary Material), so it cannot be attributed to participants using a different browser at home than in the lab.
Absolute CoG values are therefore not comparable across recording environments.

Moreover, a speaker's CoG in one environment hardly predicted their CoG in the other, as the homelab agreement was poor for /s/ (ICC(A,1) = .39/.36 for naming/reading) and essentially absent for /f/ (ICC(A,1) = .03/.04; Section 4.4), so home recordings did not even preserve the ranking of speakers.
Supervision.
The clearest and most practically relevant finding is the consistent absence of a supervision effect.

In all three acoustic measures, both tasks, and both environments, supervised and unsupervised participants produced comparable values, and Supervision did not interact with Environment or Frequency in any model.
This suggests that neither social facilitation nor monitoringinduced performance anxiety affected the spectral or temporal properties of speech production.

This contrasts with our preregistered expectation (based on Zajonc, 1965; Belletier et al., 2015) that supervision would modulate the acoustic measures and the frequency effect but is consistent with prior work showing supervision-independent replication of lexical effects on response times (Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This contrasts with our preregistered expectation (based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Zajonc, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Belletier et al., 2015)</ref> that supervision would modulate the acoustic measures and the frequency effect but is consistent with prior work showing supervision-independent replication of lexical effects on response times <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hilbig, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Piazza et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present study extends this result, for the first time, to acousticphonetic measures.

Notably, even the home-supervised condition, in which monitoring via webcam might have created a tension between domestic comfort and awareness of being observed, produced data statistically similar to the other conditions.

For researchers, this has practical consequences: online supervision via webcam remains a viable option to ensure protocol compliance without a laboratory visit, but it can also be dropped without compromising the quality of the acoustic data.
To summarize, the recording environment affected all three measures, but to different degrees and plausibly for different reasons, whereas supervision affected none.
Vowel space and voiceless VOT were slightly reduced at home; these small differences are compatible with a more relaxed speaking style.

Fricative CoG, in contrast, was substantially shifted at home, most likely by the recording equipment (consumer-grade microphones at home vs. a high-quality microphone in the lab) and environmental noise.
At the level of individual speakers, home-lab agreement was moderate for vowel space and voiceless VOT, good for /d/ prevoicing, and very poor for CoG (Section 4.4, Table 10).

text.text: Home recordings preserve group-level and within-speaker patterns better than they reproduce a given speaker's values.

Absolute values should therefore not be pooled or compared across environments without caution, especially for CoG, whereas the presence of an experimenter, in the lab or via webcam, is not needed to obtain comparable acoustic data.

Since this analysis was exploratory, future research manipulating PND across tasks and conditions is needed to confirm these findings.
VOT and CoG.
Lexical frequency did not modulate VOT or CoG in any task, environment or supervision group.
Previous frequency effects on VOT have been reported for English voiceless plosives (VanDam et al., 2009; VanDam & Port, 2005), which are aspirated with long-lag VOT.
text.formatted: Previous frequency effects on VOT have been reported for English voiceless plosives <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(VanDam et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">VanDam & Port, 2005)</ref>, which are aspirated with long-lag VOT.

text.text: Spanish voiceless plosives, however, are unaspirated and show relatively little VOT variability, making them a less informative test case.

By contrast, voiced stops in true-voicing languages like Spanish can be produced with a wide range of VOT values (e.g., Colina, 2020; Hualde, 2025; Rosner et al., 2000; Souganidis et al., 2024; Stoehr et al., 2025) and may therefore be more sensitive to frequency effects (see the exploratory analysis of /d/ in the Supplementary Material).
text.formatted: By contrast, voiced stops in true-voicing languages like Spanish can be produced with a wide range of VOT values (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Colina, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hualde, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rosner et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Souganidis et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Stoehr et al., 2025)</ref> and may therefore be more sensitive to frequency effects (see the exploratory analysis of /d/ in the Supplementary Material).

text.text: Future research should explicitly manipulate voicing and frequency to clarify how language-specific phonetic properties interact with lexical variables in VOT production.
On the other hand, this is the first investigation of lexical frequency effects on fricative CoG to our knowledge.

We hypothesized that speakers would produce HF words with a more central CoG, but the effect did not reach significance in either task; given the size of the environment artifact, a small psycholinguistic modulation would be difficult to detect at home.

Because these null results held in the lab as well as at home, they do not speak against home recordings; rather, they indicate that lexical frequency is not a suitable benchmark for these two measures in Spanish.
The frequency effect on vowel space in naming and the (exploratory) PND effect in both tasks emerged in all environments and supervision groups, although the PND effect was somewhat smaller at home.
Frequency effects were absent for VOT and CoG in both environments, so they could not serve as a benchmark for these measures.

Overall, lexical frequency proved a weaker and less consistent probe of acoustic variation than phonological neighborhood density, and a null or reversed frequency effect on a given measure cannot, by itself, be taken as evidence that home recording failed.
All participants completed both a laboratory and a home session and may thus have become familiar with the protocol.

Although the order was counterbalanced, we assessed the PND effect (the strongest effect we observed) on vowel space at home, restricting the sample to participants who completed their home session before any laboratory exposure (N = 48): the effect remained significant in both tasks (naming: t(48) = 8.85; reading: t(48) = 6.67; both p < .001; Supplementary Material), also when restricted to the unsupervised group (N = 26), suggesting that the validity of home recordings does not depend on prior laboratory familiarity.
text.formatted: Although the order was counterbalanced, we assessed the PND effect (the strongest effect we observed) on vowel space at home, restricting the sample to participants who completed their home session before any laboratory exposure (N = 48): the effect remained significant in both tasks (naming: t(48) = 8.85; reading: t(48) = 6.67; both p < .001; Supplementary Material), also when restricted to the unsupervised group (N = 26), suggesting that the validity of home recordings does not depend on prior laboratory familiarity.

text.text: Additionally, to be as close as possible to realistic remote recording, the home equipment was not controlled and participants could use any device, so we cannot separate the contributions of microphones and room acoustics to the Environment effects.
Future studies could address this by providing participants with a standard headset.
This study used a picture naming and a reading aloud task to test whether speech acoustics recorded online at home, with or without an experimenter, reproduce laboratory patterns.
The answer is measure-specific (Table 10 summarizes our recommendations by measure).
text.formatted: The answer is measure-specific (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_9">10</ref> summarizes our recommendations by measure).

text.text: Compared with the lab, vowel spaces were slightly smaller at home (significantly so in reading only), voiceless VOT was shorter, and fricative CoG was markedly higher, the latter most likely reflecting recording artifacts.
Experimenter supervision had no effect on any measure, in the lab or at home.

Psycholinguistic effects on vowel space were detected in both environments: lexical frequency in naming and, in exploratory analyses, phonological neighborhood density in both tasks, with a slightly smaller effect at home.
Lexical frequency did not affect VOT or CoG in either environment.
These findings suggest that, for some speech production studies, unsupervised home recording is a viable alternative to the lab.
Vowel measures are suitable for group-level and withinspeaker comparisons in within-subject designs, although individual vowel spaces agreed only moderately across environments.
VOT should be compared within, not across, recording environments, and voiced and voiceless plosives may be affected differently.
Fricative CoG is not recommended for remote studies without controlled equipment.
Remote paradigms can therefore support speech production research, provided that the choice of acoustic measure takes into account its sensitivity to recording conditions.

Vowel space.

Vowel space was smaller at home than in the lab in both tasks; the difference reached significance in reading (lab-home = 0.61 Bark², Cohen's d = 0.15) and went in the same direction only numerically in naming.

This direction is in line with our preregistered expectation that less controlled sessions would elicit less hyperarticulated vowels, although the reduction emerged as an overall Environment effect rather than specifically in the home-unsupervised condition.

A more relaxed speaking style at home, with less articulatory effort, therefore, could explain the reduction we observed, whereas the formal laboratory environment may induce more careful, hyperarticulated speech.
It is opposite, however, to the wider Spanish-Basque vowel space observed at home by Stoehr et al. (2023).
text.formatted: It is opposite, however, to the wider Spanish-Basque vowel space observed at home by <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Stoehr et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in recording setup may have contributed to the discrepancy between the two studies.
In Stoehr et al. (2023), lab sessions were recorded with a dedicated recorder, whereas online sessions were recorded through a web-based tool on participants' own devices.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Stoehr et al. (2023)</ref>, lab sessions were recorded with a dedicated recorder, whereas online sessions were recorded through a web-based tool on participants' own devices.

text.text: Recording software and file format therefore differed between their two environments.

In our study, both sessions were recorded through the same browser-based platform (PCIbex) and saved in the same format (WebM), so differences in recording software or file format cannot explain our Environment effect; only the microphones differed (a headset in the lab, participants' own devices at home).

Home recordings were also more variable; the standard deviation of vowel space was larger at home than in the lab for both naming (home: M = 8.46 Bark², SD = 3.24 vs. lab: M = 9.01 Bark², SD = 2.39) and reading (home: M = 8.43 Bark², SD = 3.28 vs. lab: M = 9.07 Bark², SD = 2.26; see Table 1), in line with previous research showing that online experiments typically introduce greater variability (Bürki, 2025).
text.formatted: Home recordings were also more variable; the standard deviation of vowel space was larger at home than in the lab for both naming (home: M = 8.46 Bark², SD = 3.24 vs. lab: M = 9.01 Bark², SD = 2.39) and reading (home: M = 8.43 Bark², SD = 3.28 vs. lab: M = 9.07 Bark², SD = 2.26; see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), in line with previous research showing that online experiments typically introduce greater variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bürki, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the Environment effect was small relative to the differences between speakers.
In fact, in all vowel models, most of the variance was accounted for by participants (R²c ≥ .95 vs.
R²m ≤ .06; Tables 2, 5, 6 and 9).
However, speakers' vowel spaces were only moderately preserved across environments (ICC(A,1) = .52 / .56 for naming / reading; Section 4.4).
Together with the larger variability at home, this indicates that home recordings preserve group-Vowel space.
In naming, lexical frequency modulated vowel space in both environments and supervision groups, with similar effect sizes at home and in the lab (Cohen's d = 0.14 and 0.19).
Surprisingly, however, HF words were produced with wider vowel spaces than LF words, contrary to our hypothesis (Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004) but in line with Tomaschek et al. (2014).
text.formatted: Surprisingly, however, HF words were produced with wider vowel spaces than LF words, contrary to our hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Munson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Munson & Solomon, 2004)</ref> but in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tomaschek et al. (2014)</ref>.

text.text: In reading, the effect was very small (d = 0.04) and was present at home but not in the lab, contrary to our preregistered expectation of comparable effects in both environments.
The larger frequency effect in naming is in line with the greater role of frequency in lexical access in picture naming (Mousikou & Rastle, 2015).
text.formatted: The larger frequency effect in naming is in line with the greater role of frequency in lexical access in picture naming <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mousikou & Rastle, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Since the effect emerged in naming in all recording conditions, the vowelspace measure collected at home appears sensitive enough to detect within-subject psycholinguistic effects of this size.

The unexpected direction of the frequency effect led us to examine the stimuli, which revealed that HF words tended to have more phonological neighbors than LF words (Spearman's r = .33 and .24 in naming and reading).

High-density neighborhoods impose greater phonological competition during production, driving speakers toward more peripheral, hyperarticulated vowels to maximize contrast (Scarborough, 2013; Wright et al., 2004; Hameau et al., 2021), indicating that the direction of a frequency effect on vowel space likely depends on how frequency and density covary in the stimuli.
text.formatted: High-density neighborhoods impose greater phonological competition during production, driving speakers toward more peripheral, hyperarticulated vowels to maximize contrast <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Scarborough, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Wright et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hameau et al., 2021)</ref>, indicating that the direction of a frequency effect on vowel space likely depends on how frequency and density covary in the stimuli.

text.text: Accordingly, our exploratory analyses showed that High-PND words elicited wider vowel spaces than Low-PND words in both tasks, environments and supervision groups, with larger effects (Cohen's d = 0.35 and 0.34 in naming and reading) and more variance explained by the fixed effects (R²m) than for frequency.
The PND effect, however, was smaller at home than in the lab in both tasks (naming: d = 0.31 vs.
0.39; reading: d = 0.30 vs.
This reduction parallels the smaller vowel spaces at home discussed above.
Accordingly, if speakers hyperarticulate less at home, there may also be less room for density-driven expansion.
